# Getting career-ready: Tilly's film and television journey at Solent

25 November 2026

Recent BA (Hons) Film and Television graduate Tilly made the most of her time at Solent through hands-on learning opportunities, using the industry-standard facilities and making the most of Southampton as a great city.

Tilly first visited Southampton Solent University as a student and knew it was the right fit for her.

"When I was in college, I was studying film and television. We went to visit Solent University for the day and the lecturers there, they showed us around the live TV studio rooms and the university as a whole. After this trip I was so excited.

I knew that Solent was where I wanted to go after I finished college. So later on that year I visited an open day, and I got to speak to the lecturers on the film and television course and got to know the course more in-depth."

A key selling point for Tilly was the balance between practical based learning and theory, allowing students to practise the type of work they want to get into.

"In the end I chose to do film and television at Solent University. This was because there was a 50/50 split in the course so it was half practical and half theory and analysis.

Honestly this stood out to me compared to other courses, because at the start I wasn't sure on which one I wanted to do. Having the aspects of both practical and theory really helped us out.

For me film and television at Solent covers all elements of film and TV, so when leaving university, I have a much better idea of which department I want to work in after I finished."

Coming from a small village, the move to Southampton also gave Tilly the opportunity to explore somewhere new and broaden her creative interests.

"As I was raised in a small village in the Midlands, there were never many job opportunities for me and not many places I could broaden my creative interests. This is exactly what Solent stood out for me and this was just a personal choice for me, but I wanted to be by the coast. Honestly this was a win-win situation for me. A great course with a great view. One of my favourite things about Southampton is how everything is in such short walking distance."

Her course also gives her the opportunity to get hands-on with facilities that reflect the changing film and television industry, including Solent's virtual production screen.

"Having a virtual production screen at university creates such a unique learning experience for me. As virtual production screens are recently new, I feel so lucky to train on one in my course."

University has given Tilly more than just the opportunity to develop her creative skills. It's helped her become more independent, gain work experience, make friends for life and build connections that could support her future career.

"For any future career in the industry it's almost necessary to have hands-on experience on your CV, and connections too. Solent has built up my CV so well, because whilst learning the theoretical aspects behind film, I'm also getting practical and professional experience before I face the big wide world.

For my final year at Solent we had to complete a final major project and we chose to do a short film – this was an incredible experience for me. I'd helped out with films before, but making our own made us understand so many forgotten aspects of creating a film."

Reflecting on her time at Solent so far, Tilly has some advice for anyone starting their own university journey.

"If there's one thing I can tell someone who's just started at university, it's make the most of it! Get as much work experience as you can, step outside your comfort zone and have fun. Solent has given me a step into an industry with experience under my belt and that's what I'm looking forward to in the future, whatever it holds."

# How to Assess Your Organisation's Data Readiness for AI

Before investing in AI, it's important to understand whether your organisation's data is ready. Explore five key areas to assess, from data quality and system integration to governance and workforce skills, and discover where to prioritise improvements.

- Message

Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities for organisations to improve efficiency, automate processes and make better-informed decisions. However, the effectiveness of these technologies often depends on something businesses already have: their data.

Inconsistent records, disconnected systems and unclear data governance can limit how effectively AI applications perform. As organisations explore opportunities to integrate AI into their operations, understanding the quality and accessibility of their existing information is an important starting point.

Assessing data readiness can help businesses identify potential obstacles, prioritise improvements and make more informed decisions about where to invest in AI.

## What Does Data Readiness for AI Mean?

Data readiness refers to how well an organisation’s existing data can support its intended uses, including AI-powered tools and applications.

For AI to generate reliable insights, support decision-making or automate processes effectively, it needs access to information that is accurate, relevant and appropriately managed.

This involves several considerations:

- Data quality: Is information accurate, complete and consistent?
- Data accessibility: Can the people and systems that need information access it?
- Data integration: Can different systems share information effectively?
- Data governance: Are clear processes in place to manage and protect information?
- Workforce capability: Do employees have the skills to manage and use data effectively?

Organisations don’t necessarily need to resolve every data challenge before introducing AI. The level of readiness required depends on the intended application.

A team using AI to support content creation will have different requirements from an organisation developing AI-powered financial forecasting.

The starting point is understanding what you want AI to achieve and whether your existing data can support that objective.

## Five Questions to Assess Your Organisation’s Data Readiness for AI

#### 1. Do You Know What Data Your Organisation Holds and Where It Lives?

Most organisations collect substantial amounts of information through their everyday operations.

Customer records, financial transactions and operational reports may be stored across multiple systems, spreadsheets and departmental databases. Over time, this can create fragmented environments where different teams maintain separate versions of the same information.

For businesses implementing AI, accessing the right information can become complicated, particularly when applications rely on data from multiple departments.

For example, an organisation introducing AI-powered sales forecasting may need information from its CRM, finance platform and reporting systems. If those sources are difficult to locate or reconcile, developing reliable forecasts becomes more challenging.

Meanwhile, at James Paget NHS Trust, data apprentices have supported data cleansing and validation as part of a wider data migration project, helping the organisation improve how it manages and uses information.

Where to start: Identify the information required for your proposed AI application. Establish where it is stored, who manages it and whether other departments maintain separate versions.

Creating an inventory of relevant data sources can help identify gaps, duplication and opportunities to improve information management.

#### 2. How Accurate and Reliable Is Your Data?

To assess data quality, review whether the information needed for your AI application is accurate, complete, consistent and up to date. Look for duplicated records, missing information and conflicting definitions that could affect the reliability of AI-generated outputs.

AI systems depend on the information available to them. When that information is incomplete, inconsistent or outdated, the quality of their outputs can suffer.

Customer records may contain duplicate entries, reporting systems may use inconsistent categories, or information may be updated at different intervals across departments.

Consider a business using AI to analyse customer purchasing behaviour.

If its records contain missing transactions or outdated customer information, the resulting analysis may provide a misleading picture of customer activity. The AI might process the available information correctly while still producing conclusions that don’t reflect the reality of the business.

Another consideration is whether AI applications have sufficient context to interpret organisational information accurately.

Businesses often have their own terminology, definitions and ways of categorising information. For example, if departments use different definitions of an ‘active customer’, AI-generated analysis could vary depending on which definition is applied.

Where to start: Review a sample of the data relevant to your intended AI application.

Look for missing information, duplicated records, outdated entries and inconsistent definitions. Establish whether employees share an understanding of what key data fields represent.

Addressing these issues early can improve confidence in the information used to support decisions.

#### 3. Can Your Systems Share Information Effectively?

Even when organisations have reliable data, they may struggle to use it effectively if their systems operate independently.

Many businesses rely on multiple platforms to manage different activities. Sales teams might use a CRM, finance teams may work within accounting software, and operational departments could maintain separate reporting platforms.

When these systems don’t communicate, employees often become responsible for transferring information between them.

This can involve exporting spreadsheets, combining datasets or repeatedly entering the same information into different platforms.

These processes create additional work, increase the possibility of errors and can limit opportunities for AI-powered automation.

For example, an organisation might want to automate management reporting using information from several departments. However, disconnected systems could mean employees still need to manually gather and prepare information before AI can process it.

We encountered similar challenges within Baltic’s own data team. By improving our data infrastructure, we were able to automate previously manual processes and save 110 working hours per month across multiple teams.

Where to start: Map how information moves between the systems involved in your proposed AI application.

Identify where employees manually transfer information, where duplication occurs and whether existing platforms offer integration capabilities.

This can help establish which improvements would deliver the greatest operational benefit.

#### 4. Are Appropriate Data Governance and Security Measures in Place?

As organisations introduce AI into everyday operations, they need to consider how information is accessed, processed and protected.

Data governance refers to the policies, responsibilities and processes that determine how an organisation manages its information.

This includes establishing who owns particular datasets, who can access them and what controls apply to their use.

These considerations become particularly important when AI applications connect to internal systems or process commercially sensitive and personal information.

Businesses need to understand what information an AI application requires, how that information will be processed and whether appropriate safeguards are in place.

Without clear guidance, employees may be uncertain about which information can be shared with AI platforms, what requires human verification or who is accountable for the resulting outputs.

Effective governance helps organisations establish consistent approaches to these decisions, supporting responsible AI adoption.

Where to start: Review existing policies around data access, security and AI use.

Establish who is responsible for approving the use of organisational data within AI applications and whether employees understand the relevant requirements.

Where third-party providers are involved, assess how information will be stored, processed and protected.

#### 5. Does Your Workforce Have the Skills to Manage and Use Data Effectively?

An organisation’s data readiness also depends on the capabilities of its workforce.

Employees need the knowledge and skills to maintain accurate information, interpret data, manage systems and identify opportunities to improve existing processes.

As organisations adopt more sophisticated AI applications, these responsibilities can become increasingly complex.

For example, implementing AI-powered reporting may require employees who can assess data quality, connect information from different sources and evaluate whether the resulting outputs are reliable.

Research reinforces the importance of developing these capabilities.

McKinsey’s State of AI Trust in 2026 research identified knowledge and training gaps as a significant barrier to implementing responsible AI practices, with 59% of respondents identifying them as an obstacle.

For employers, this highlights the importance of workforce development alongside investment in new technologies.

Improving data literacy can help employees recognise potential issues and interpret information confidently. Developing specialist capabilities in data analysis and data engineering can also help businesses improve the systems and processes supporting AI adoption.

Where to start: Assess the data skills available within your organisation and identify gaps that could affect proposed AI projects.

Consider whether employees can manage information effectively, develop integrations, assess data quality and interpret AI-generated outputs.

This will help determine where additional training or specialist expertise may be required.

## Where Should Organisations Start Improving Their Data Readiness for AI?

Improving data readiness doesn’t have to involve reviewing every system and dataset across your organisation.

Start by identifying a specific business process that could benefit from AI, such as reporting, forecasting or administrative automation. Consider what information the application would need and assess it against the five areas outlined above.

This can help identify which improvements should take priority.

For example, a business exploring AI-powered reporting might discover that inconsistent information across departments is its biggest obstacle. Standardising how data is recorded and shared could be a more valuable first step than investing in new technology.

By focusing on a defined use case, organisations can make targeted improvements, evaluate their effectiveness and build on those foundations as their AI ambitions develop.

## Building the Data Capability to Support AI Adoption

As AI becomes increasingly integrated into business operations, the quality, accessibility and management of organisational data will continue to influence how effectively these technologies can be used.

Assessing data readiness helps employers understand their existing capabilities, identify areas for improvement and make more informed decisions about future investment.

Developing the right workforce skills is an important part of this process.

At Baltic Apprenticeships, we help organisations develop the practical data skills needed to improve information quality, streamline processes and make better-informed business decisions.

Our data apprenticeship programmes support the development of capabilities across data analysis, data engineering and related disciplines, helping employers build the internal expertise needed to make better use of their information.

# CIMA Level 7 Apprenticeships Are Closing to New Starters: What Are Your Options for 2027?

For many employers, the CIMA Level 7 apprenticeship has been an important route for developing finance talent. With CIMA confirming that it will stop accepting new registrations onto the Level 7 apprenticeship expected from December 2026, organisations across the UK are now reviewing their future training and recruitment plans.

If you’ve relied on the CIMA Level 7 apprenticeship to develop your finance team, now is the time to plan how you will train your next finance intake. For 2027 and beyond, you may consider an ACCA Level 7 apprenticeship for eligible trainees. For those who are ineligible for level 7 funding, a Level 4 apprenticeship can support progression to employer-funded ACCA or CIMA training

What is changing?

Following changes to apprenticeship standards introduced by Skills England, CIMA has announced that it will no longer accept new entrants onto the Level 7 apprenticeship programme from 18 December 2026. Existing apprentices already enrolled on programme will continue to be supported through to completion.

This means employers recruiting future finance trainees will need to consider alternative apprenticeship or qualification routes.

What training options are available for your next intake?

The right pathway will depend on the role you’re recruiting for, the experience of the learner and the funding available.

ACCA Level 7 Apprenticeship

For many employers, the ACCA Level 7 apprenticeship offers the closest alternative to the CIMA apprenticeship route. This pathway combines professional accountancy training with practical workplace experience offering an option for eligible trainees whose roles would benefit from a broad accountancy qualification and an exam-based route.

In England, Level 7 apprenticeship funding is generally available to trainees aged 16-21 when they start their apprenticeship. Trainees aged 22-24 can also qualify if they have an Education, Health and Care plan or are in or have been in local authority care.

Level 4 Accounting Technician Apprenticeship

For trainees starting their finance careers, the Level 4 Accounting Technician apprenticeship can provide a strong foundation in accounting and finance. Employers often use this route to:

- Develop school leavers

- Build internal finance talent pipelines

- Support employees moving into finance roles

Eligible learners aged 22 and over can still access Level 4 apprenticeship funding. After Level 4, employers can fund further ACCA study where it suits the trainee’s role.

Employer-Funded ACCA Tuition

Some organisations may prefer to fund professional qualifications directly rather than through an apprenticeship programme.

Employers can pay directly for ACCA tuition, with classroom and online options available. This is also an option for trainees who aren’t eligible for Level 7 funding.

Commercially Funded CIMA Routes

While the Level 7 apprenticeship route is closing to new starters, First Intuition will continue to support learners who wish to pursue CIMA through commercially funded study options, including traditional exam-based routes delivered through Online Live classes and the CGMA Finance Leadership Programme (FLP).

This provides an alternative for organisations that remain committed to developing talent through the CIMA pathway.

Why are employers considering ACCA?

Many employers who have historically chosen CIMA are now reviewing whether ACCA could better support their future workforce needs and succession planning objectives.

ACCA develops knowledge and skills across:

- Financial reporting

- Financial management

- Management accounting

- Audit and assurance

- Taxation

- Business strategy

From the September 2027 exam session, trainees at Strategic Professional level will choose one option exam from five. For example; Performance and Insights Professional may suit management accountants who support business decisions and report on performance.

Additional benefits of ACCA include:

- Access to Level 7 apprenticeship funding for eligible learners.

- A traditional exam-based assessment structure.

- Eligible ACCA Approved Employers can simplify how trainees record their practical experience objectives.

What should employers compare before making a decision?

Before choosing a pathway, employers should compare funding eligibility, total cost, study format and time to qualification to ensure the option aligns with both learner needs and business objectives.

Frequently Asked Questions

When will CIMA stop accepting new Level 7 apprentices, and what happens to existing apprentices?

CIMA is expected to stop accepting new registrations to the Level 7 apprenticeship from 18 December 2026. Existing apprentices can continue studying and complete their programme, with First Intuition continuing to support them through to qualification.

Can my trainees still study CIMA with First Intuition in 2027?

Yes. First Intuition will continue to offer commercially funded CIMA study options in 2027, including Online Live tuition and the CGMA Finance Leadership Programme (FLP).

What are the alternatives to the CIMA Level 7 apprenticeship?

For many employers, the ACCA Level 7 apprenticeship is the closest alternative. Other options may include commercially funded ACCA or CIMA pathways, depending on the learner’s role, experience, career goals and funding eligibility.

Who qualifies for ACCA Level 7 apprenticeship funding in England?

Level 7 apprenticeship funding is generally available to trainees aged 16-21 when they start their apprenticeship. Trainees aged 22-24 can also qualify if they have an Education, Health and Care plan or are in, or have been in, local authority care.

title: Meet our Trailblazers - Everton Sutherland-Adebiyi | The University of Law

7 mins read

Meet Everton Sutherland-Adebiyi, an MA Law student at our London Bloomsbury campus. Read on to learn more about his experience as a care leaver, his ambitions to become a barrister and how he hopes to use his experiences to guide others in the future.

By Abbie Wilson. Published 25 November 2026.

## What inspired you to study a law degree?

My background, experiences of injustice and determination to understand and challenge systems led me towards law.

My experience hasn’t been without significant challenges, but I remain determined to realise that potential and contribute towards making those opportunities genuinely accessible to others.

## Why study at The University of Law?

The clue is in the name. I wanted specialist legal education that would prepare me for professional practice. I was also drawn to the University’s promise of helping students achieve their potential.

## What are some of your recent accomplishments and what do they mean to you?

Being shortlisted for the National Diversity Awards and graduating from my undergraduate degree have been significant milestones in my career so far.

I’ve also contributed to local and national discussions on policy, justice and accountability, helping identify gaps, develop solutions and influence how services support vulnerable young people. My work spans local government, corporate parenting, youth participation, school governance and equality representation.

Most recently, I became Co-Chair of the University’s Disabled Students’ Network. For me, achievement isn’t simply recognition or holding a title. It’s turning ideas into practical solutions that improve people’s lives.

## Who has had the biggest impact on your experience at The University of Law?

Salomé Verrell and Fred Price have made a significant difference. Both recognised my academic potential and provided meaningful support when barriers threatened my ability to continue studying. I would not still be in The University of Law if it was not for these two individuals.

I’ve also benefited from the excellent teaching and passion demonstrated by my lecturer, Jodie McCarty. Their actions reinforce something I strongly believe; policies alone don’t change lives. People who listen, understand and act do. Sometimes one professional can make the difference between someone continuing their education and falling through the cracks.

## How has your lived experience of care impacted your career and study choices?

My experiences of injustice have fuelled my ambition to become a Barrister.

As a Black male with care experience, I’ve witnessed how stereotypes, discrimination and institutional barriers can intersect. Only around 15% of young people from care backgrounds progress to university by age 19, compared with approximately 47% of their peers. That disparity should concern us all.

Law provides an opportunity to challenge injustice, protect rights and influence systems. My lived experience shapes my perspective, but my ambition is to succeed on merit and use that professional competence to create meaningful change.

## What kept you motivated on the difficult days of balancing study and caring responsibilities?

My reason why.

Always remember your why. Don’t justify it, never apologise for it, and never forget it.

However, motivation alone isn’t always enough. Oxford research found that more than one in six care leavers withdraw from higher education. Care-experienced students can face additional pressures, including housing insecurity, financial hardship, loneliness and mental health challenges.

Birthdays, Christmas and university holidays can be particularly isolating when you don’t have a traditional family support network or somewhere to return to. Some international and estranged students experience similar isolation.

Universities must recognise that belonging and support should extend beyond the classroom and academic calendar.

## How have you overcome self-doubt or setbacks?

In my journey so far, many of my setbacks have involved circumstances outside my control, including barriers within systems that were supposed to support me. From this, I developed my own philosophy: control what you can, plan for what you cannot, and prepare as much as possible to minimise the impact.

My best advice for others when facing self-doubt or setbacks is to take ownership of your journey, hold others accountable, and don’t be afraid to hold yourself accountable too. Importantly, wait for no-one.

## What’s the one thing you’ve achieved that you never thought you would?

I wouldn’t describe myself as successful just yet. There are still ambitions to fulfil and wrongs I’m working to put right. However, one thing I’ve achieved is a sense of clarity and ownership over my future. I’ve learnt that I don’t need anyone’s permission to prosper, nor should I apologise for pursuing what I believe in. My circumstances may have shaped my journey, but they don’t get to dictate or limit my destination.

Importantly, this isn’t my story. It’s merely one part of it. My story is complicated, and in many respects, I’m still finding the words to tell it.

That’s partly what inspired my care experienced storytelling book project, which is currently inviting expressions of interest. I want to help others take ownership of their narratives, challenge stereotypes and demonstrate to the next generation that success isn’t always a linear journey.

## When you picture your future, what do you see?

My priority is to qualify as a Barrister as soon as practicable. The further I progress, the more injustice I encounter, and the more determined I become to advocate for people whose voices are overlooked. I recognise the limitations of my current position, which is why gaining the necessary qualifications and professional expertise matters.

Injustice may never disappear entirely, but that doesn’t mean we stop challenging it.

My approach remains simple: stay focused, stay busy and stay effective.

## Important information for employers

Welcome to our information page for employers of AI and Automation apprentices. If you require further information, please email the Apprenticeships Unit. Alternatively, please call (+44) 0161 247 3720 between 9:00am – 4:30pm Monday to Friday.

You play a crucial role in supporting your apprentice’s learning and identifying opportunities for the development of their digital and technology skills. We are keen for you to play an active role in the apprenticeship. Please bookmark this page as it is regularly updated.

### Line manager and mentor information

Our briefings for line managers and mentors help you understand how to support your apprentice’s development. You can meet key members of our team and learn more about the course, so that you can plan the apprentice’s workplace experience, and get the most from their assignments, research and project work.

These sessions include:

- introduction to the Manchester Met Apprenticeships Unit
- course structure, content, delivery and assessment
- the role of a workplace manager or mentor
- supporting apprentice learners
- The development of knowledge, skills & behaviours
- engaging with the e-portfolio

A booking link for the next session will be added here once confirmed.

### Work-based projects

All apprentices undertake a synoptic work-based project towards the end of their apprenticeship which forms a crucial part of the end-point assessment process. The synoptic project is a significant live project, managed in the workplace by the apprentice across a substantial period (usually around 6 months). It should be aligned to organisational need and demonstrate strategic impact and return on investment.

- AI and Automation teaching dates (to be added shortly)

Apprentices will access their timetables through their virtual learning environment, once they have enrolled. Moodle provides the most up-to-date and accurate timetable information for apprentices, including assessment deadlines.

### Apprenticeship Standard and assessment information

The apprenticeship standardprovides the building blocks of the AI and Automation Apprenticeship. It is the blueprint for the development of our apprentices across the duration of the course. The standard will be used regularly during reviews as a point of reference, and we recommend that you familiarise yourself with its contents.

### Units overview

AI Foundation and Responsible Practice

### AI Foundation and Responsible Practice

In this module, you will develop an understanding of the core concepts of AI and automation and explore how they are used in modern workplaces to improve processes and ways of working. You will learn how AI and automation can be applied safely, effectively, and responsibly within organisational contexts.

The module will introduce you to programming fundamentals, focusing on simple logic and practical coding activities that support basic automation tasks. You will also explore ethical, legal, and governance considerations, including data protection, risk, and accountability, while examining how responsible and sustainable AI practices can support organisational goals and socially responsible decision-making.

Designing and Developing AI-enabled Automation Solution

### Designing and Developing AI-enabled Automation Solution

This module develops practical, hands-on skills to build, test and improve AI enabled automation solutions in the workplace. You will focus on turning identified opportunities into working automation by analysing workflows, configuring integrations and developing automated solutions using low code or no code tools. The module concentrates on technical implementation rather than strategy, ethics or change management. You will test, monitor and refine automation solutions, preparing them for use in a live environment through clear documentation, re-testing and basic handover processes.

Human Centred AI, Adoption and Change

### Human Centred AI, Adoption and Change

This module focuses on the successful adoption of AI and automation within organisations, with an emphasis on people, processes and change. You will examine how work is carried out across teams and how AI enabled change affects roles, responsibilities and day to day practices. The module develops practical skills in communication, collaboration and supporting teams through change. You will examine barriers to adoption, evaluate the impact of automation on people and processes, and identify continuous improvement opportunities to ensure AI and automation deliver sustainable organisational value.

Synoptic Project

### Synoptic Project

The synoptic project module brings together the knowledge and skills developed across the programme and applies them to a realistic workplace scenario. You will identify an automation opportunity, design and develop a solution, and test and refine it in response to user and organisational needs. The module emphasises ethical practice, governance, stakeholder engagement, and clear communication across the full lifecycle of AI and automation solutions. This approach aligns with key assessment outcomes such as solution design, evaluation, risk management, and continuous improvement, enabling you to demonstrate applied competence.

# Charlotte Johnson

Charlotte is a Nursing Associate apprentice who balances work, study and life. Here's how Solent shaped her future in healthcare.

Job title:Nursing Associate Apprentice

Employer:Colten Care

Studied:FdSc Nursing Associate

## So, Charlotte, who are you and how did you end up at Solent?

I'm a second-year Nursing Associate apprentice. I came to Solent from my workplace, after years in care homes and community healthcare. It was a last-minute decision, so I had no time to visit. A colleague who knew the course well reassured me it would be hugely beneficial, and she was right.

## What made you realise Solent was the right place?

My workplace made the decision, so it was out of my hands. Once I knew, I researched the University and the degree. After my first day, I knew I'd love it. I thoroughly enjoyed the ice-breaking activities on our first day. Those helped me find my way around campus and make friends who I'll likely keep for the rest of my life.

## What makes your lecturers different?

They understand what it's like to be an apprentice and how extra pressures affect us as learners. They constantly link theory to practice and create a safe space for us to share our experiences. That's been invaluable for understanding the content and knowing I can apply it properly in my work.

I want to say a sincere thank you to all my lecturers for their guidance and support over the past two years. Their teaching, encouragement and patience have shaped my confidence and helped me grow academically and professionally. I'm truly grateful for everything they’ve done, and I'll carry their lessons with me throughout my nursing career.

## Is your degree preparing you for a real nursing career?

It's taught me far more about nursing than I expected, and so much about myself and what I'm capable of. I feel thoroughly prepared for my career because I understand the theories behind human behaviour and the evidence-based practice involved in everyday nursing.

## What hands-on experience have you had?

Through university connections and placements, I've played an active part in critical incidents in practice and appeared on a national podcast about my service improvement project. As a course rep, I supported my peers, and I was thrilled to win the Student Union's Course Rep of the Year award. It really validated the effort I'd put in.

## What's made you go "wow" so far?

The Anatomage table blew my mind. I'm fascinated by how far nursing education technology has come. Every time I pass an assignment or project, I get another "wow" moment, because I'm making the most of being a Solent apprentice. I'm also constantly in awe of the opportunities I've been given over the past two years.

The Anatomage tables and human health labs are the best part. Using them has been a unique experience, and they've helped me practise the clinical skills in my proficiencies.

## What's the most important thing you've learned?

How much active listening is worth, and how much you learn from it. Healthcare feels fast-paced and task-focused, but slowing down and listening to your patient or resident can improve their health and wellbeing.

Nursing is so much more than a job. It's a vocation that applies to the people in your care and everyone you care about. I love how applicable the content is to both work and life. I'm looking forward to using what I've learned to make a real difference.

## Did Solent have your back when things got tough?

Absolutely. This year was particularly hard because a close family member was unwell. I can't fault the Student Hub or my academic assessors. Following the support pathways my academic team guided me to, I got help without it affecting my performance or opportunities, and without judgement.

## What will you take away from Solent?

I'd definitely recommend Solent, as there's so much to gain. I've learnt a huge amount and made really close connections with my peers. My local placements, wonderfully organised by the placements team, also gave me plenty of professional connections in the community and hospital settings, which will support my development and career opportunities.

The academic support has been beyond what I could have wished for, along with the learning resources and the connections I've made with my peers and academic teams. It's been an invaluable experience.

## What's next for your career?

My focus is adapting to my new role as a registered nursing associate, establishing myself in practice and prioritising patient care. I'm looking forward to supporting students and developing my skills. Because my degree covered all fields of nursing, I'm well placed to work with a variety of patients and settings, which I may explore further.

## How is Solent preparing you for what's ahead?

I've learnt self-directed study, which will support my continuing professional development and the revalidation process. That's on top of the wealth of information and skills I've been taught over the past two years.

# Stu Lang

Discover how Stu built a career in live sports broadcasting, working on events like the Ryder Cup.

Job title:Production Manager

Employer:Sky Sports

## Tell us a little about your career so far

When I graduated from Solent I went straight into working at ITV Emmerdale as a camera assistant when I moved back up north. Shortly after I realised that cameras wasn’t the area I wanted to go down! Around a year after graduating I started at Sky Sports as a Junior Production Coordinator across multiple sports, and a couple of months later became a full time Production Coordinator for Sky Sports Golf. I stayed on this for 5 and a half years also becoming a Senior Production Coordinator working on some amazing events like the Masters, Ryder Cup and The Open. I moved briefly over to the EFL Team as an SPC and then became a Production Manager. I have been a Production Manager for almost 2 years and have worked across Golf, Baller League and the Premier League.

## What does a typical working day look like?

I am currently a Production Manager on Sky Sports Premier League. I am responsible for all planning and delivery of the game that I am across. This includes being the main contact to the league and the clubs, along with any suppliers that we work with. Booking facilities and crew, and anything that they may need. I am on site most weekends at Premier League matches, responsible for getting them on TV and around the world, and fixing any issues as they arise!

## Why did you pick Solent?

I Attended loads of open days across the country, the minute I came to Solent I knew I wanted to go there, had a 1 on 1 chat with the lead lecturer and saw all the TV facilities that were on offer. Stayed nearby in the city as I had come down from Leeds and loved how the city it was!

## What was the best thing about your course lecturers?

The lecturers on the Television Production course are brilliant, world class in their field with huge amounts of broadcast experience. Most of all they are the most personable and caring people – making it an absolute pleasure to learn from them. Since graduating we have stayed in contact and it’s always great to catch up!

The Studios, the Edit Suites, and the TV facilities with in the building are amazing. Now working in Television and seeing the Studios and Galleries in the working world make you realise how good the facilities are at Solent.

## Can you talk a bit about any opportunities you had to get practical experience?

My favourite of the external opportunities I had while at Solent was working with Solent Productions in the summer at music festivals. I worked at Boardmasters festival – Camera Operating on the main stage for the big screens. Filming Sunday headliner George Ezra was amazing, to turn round and see thousands of people was quite an impressive sight!

## What was life like as a Solent student?

Solent life was great – you live and study so close to the city centre so it really feels like you’re part of the furniture. I was part of the Sonar TV society which was great for some extra TV experience, and the friends I lived with were all in different sports teams and they loved it!

## Do you feel like your studies helped you prepare for a career in the industry?

Absolutely – taking advantage of all the facilities, people and experience that Solent has to offer, means you are much better equipped and confident when applying for careers in the TV industry. The modules and skills you learn & study on the course are aimed to prepare you for the industry and make the transition from student into the industry much easier.

The ability to be able to rent out any kit that you want and create your own work outside of uni projects is brilliant – as you can get used to equipment you will use going forward and give you the edge when applying for jobs.

## What’s your career highlight so far?

As a Reading FC fan, the temptation to say Production Managing my first game at Reading is massive, but I can’t say that! I’ve been to some amazing golf events in my time – but I would have to say working on The Ryder Cup in Rome when Europe won in 2023. It was an unbelievable event to work on, and standing on the first tee on Sunday morning was an experience I’ll never forget! Becoming a Production Manager is my proudest moment. It was the job I wanted from the moment I started working in TV, so loving my job is my career highlight.

# CGFX Festival inspires the next generation of games, animation, CGI and VFX talent

26 November 2026

Students from schools and colleges across the south were given a glimpse into the future of games, animation, CGI and VFX at CGFX Festival, a day of industry insight and creative inspiration.

The event brings together industry professionals, successful alumni and creative experts to show students what it is really like to work in the creative industries.

Through talks, insights and real-world experiences, attendees gained an understanding of the skills, workflows and creative thinking that bring today’s games, films and digital experiences to life.

Alex Scott, Lecturer in VFX and CGI at Solent, said: “It was fantastic to see how enthusiastic the students were. There is still a lot of work to be done in raising awareness of the diverse career opportunities within VFX and CGI. While AI is changing the industry, it cannot replace the individual creativity, technical expertise and problem-solving skills that people bring to their work. Today was a great opportunity to showcase what is possible and help students see how Solent can equip them with the skills and confidence to pursue a career in these exciting industries.”

Solent graduates now working across the industry shared their experiences with students, from games and post-production to 3D visualisation.

Liz Beer, Lead Technical Animator at Funcom, was joined by Abe Naisant, VFX artist and Director of Flaneur Atelier, alongside Ciaran Lock, a Runner at award-winning post-production house ENVY.

They spoke about their roles, how students can break into the industry and how the opportunities at Solent can help them build the skills they need.

Ciaran, who has worked on productions including Celebrity Traitors and Cunk on Cinema, spoke about his journey, and the time he spent trying to land a job in the industry after graduating. He shared simple, practical ways students can improve their chances and find work sooner.

"Be persistent," he says. "There will be hurdles, but eventually you will get to where you want to be. That mindset helped me land my job as a runner."

Virtual Technologist, Sean Rodrigo showcased recent creative projects combining AI, 3D printing and digital and hand-crafted miniature techniques. His work included projects for TR Gobrazy's production Over Forreduci.

Students also had the chance to ask questions and find out more about working in the sector. Deborah Avery, Course Lead for Video Game Development at Southampton College, said:

"Bringing my students along gave them a valuable opportunity to hear directly from industry professionals and see what they could aspire to achieve. It reinforces the message I share with them about how hard work and dedication can pay off, while introducing them to potential role models and the wide range of career opportunities within the industry. It was also a great opportunity for students to network, ask questions and gain insight into the different routes into the sector."

CGFX reflects Solent’s practice-led approach to teaching, which puts industry experience at the heart of the University’s courses. Students heard directly from people working in the industry, discovered different career pathways and picked up practical advice to help them take their next steps towards a creative career.

Find out more about Solent's CGI and Visual Effects at one of our upcoming Open Days or via the Solent University website.

The accreditation was officially announced at The 5% Club’s Skills Summit on 18 November 2026, celebrating employers across the UK that are committed to developing their workforce through apprenticeships, graduate programmes and other structured ‘earn and learn’ opportunities.

## What is The 5% Club?

The 5% Club is a UK-wide movement of more than 1,300 employers committed to increasing the number, quality and range of ‘earn and learn’ opportunities available to people across the country.

Its members collectively employ more than 2.1 million people, including over 135,000 individuals participating in apprenticeships, graduate programmes and sponsored learning opportunities.

Through its annual Employer Audit, The 5% Club independently benchmarks participating organisations and recognises their commitment to workforce development through Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum accredited membership.

Gold accreditation is awarded to organisations where more than 5% of their UK workforce participates in qualifying earn-and-learn programmes, demonstrating a commitment to investing in skills and developing future talent.

In 2026, more than 286 organisations participated in the Employer Audit, representing a wide range of sectors, including technology, construction, finance, retail, defence and the public sector.

## Investing in our people and developing future talent

At Baltic, investing in people and supporting their professional development is central to the organisation’s culture and long-term success.

As a specialist apprenticeship training provider, Baltic understands the value of combining practical workplace experience with structured learning and development.

This commitment extends to its own workforce, with opportunities for colleagues to build their skills, gain qualifications, take on new responsibilities and progress in their careers.

Achieving Gold accreditation reflects Baltic’s ongoing efforts to create an environment where colleagues feel supported, valued and empowered to reach their full potential.

Beth Chainey, Director of People Growth & Culture at Baltic, said:

“We’re incredibly proud to have achieved Gold accreditation from The 5% Club. This recognition reflects our ongoing commitment to investing in our people and creating meaningful opportunities for colleagues to learn, develop and progress in their careers.

“At Baltic, we believe that developing our people is key to our success. Whether that’s through apprenticeships, professional development or opportunities for career progression, we want everyone to feel supported and empowered to reach their full potential.

“This achievement is a testament to the fantastic people we have across the business, and we look forward to continuing to build on this success by creating even more opportunities for our colleagues to grow and thrive.”

## Recognising a commitment to workplace learning

The 5% Club’s Employer Audit provides an independent assessment of how organisations recruit, develop and support individuals participating in earn-and-learn programmes.

Alongside recognising employers through its accreditation scheme, the Audit provides benchmarking insights into workforce development, including recruitment, diversity, training completion rates and future growth opportunities.

Baltic’s Gold accreditation demonstrates its commitment to providing structured development opportunities and contributing to a wider movement of employers investing in the skills and capabilities of their workforce.

Mark Cameron OBE, Chief Executive of The 5% Club, said:

“It’s been a phenomenal year for the Employer Audit. We started out with 73 participating employers back in 2021, and this year more than 286 organisations took part. Baltic’s achievement of Gold membership shows what happens when a business genuinely commits to developing its people. It’s exactly the kind of leadership that will shape the UK’s future workforce.

“This isn’t a one-off for Baltic, it’s how they operate. As more of our members reach these higher tiers each year, businesses like Baltic are helping raise the standard for workplace learning across their industries.”

## Building on our success

Achieving Gold accreditation is an important milestone for Baltic and an opportunity to celebrate the contributions of colleagues across the business.

As Baltic continues to grow and evolve, supporting its people through learning, development and career progression will remain a key priority.

## Overview

Effective virtual training involves more than moving classroom content online. Trainers and facilitators need to adapt their delivery techniques, create opportunities for participation, and use technology purposefully to support learning.

TAP® Delivering Virtual Learning (Accelerated) is a practical, one-day course for professionals who already have core training delivery and facilitation skills and want to apply them in virtual learning environments. As part of the TAP® Delivery Excellence Pathway, the programme builds on the foundations established through TAP® Training Delivery Skills and TAP® Facilitation Skills.

You will explore the factors that influence learner engagement online, adapt classroom activities for virtual delivery, and consider accessibility, inclusion, and cognitive load when designing learning experiences. You will then create and showcase a virtual learning activity on a subject of your choice, receiving structured peer and facilitator feedback against the TAP® Virtual Delivery Criteria.

The result is an opportunity to practise your virtual delivery skills, identify areas for improvement, and plan how to apply your learning in the workplace.

## Prerequisites

This course is designed for learners who have already developed core training delivery and facilitation skills through professional experience or the wider TAP® Delivery Excellence Pathway.

Before attending, you should:

- Have experience delivering or facilitating learning activities
- Identify a suitable topic for your virtual learning activity
- Have access to a virtual learning platform and appropriate technology
- Be prepared to apply your existing delivery and facilitation skills in a virtual environment

### Target audience

This accelerated virtual training course is suitable for:

- Trainers transitioning from classroom training to virtual delivery
- Facilitators looking to improve engagement and participation in online sessions
- Subject matter experts responsible for delivering learning online
- Learning and development professionals
- Internal trainers and coaches
- Professionals progressing through the TAP® Delivery Excellence Pathway

It is particularly relevant to professionals who want to make their online training more engaging, inclusive, and effective without losing the core principles of good training and facilitation.

Getting started – prerequisites and preparation

Before the programme begins, you will identify a suitable topic for your virtual learning activity and consider how to apply your existing training and facilitation skills online. You will also check that you have access to an appropriate virtual learning platform and the technology needed to participate.

This preparation provides a starting point for the practical activities throughout the day.

Foundations of virtual learning

Explore the principles of effective virtual training and the factors that shape the learner experience online.

Topics include:

- Understanding virtual and hybrid learning environments
- Exploring the virtual learner experience
- Identifying factors that affect engagement and participation
- Considering the benefits and challenges of virtual delivery
- Understanding the principles of effective virtual learning

You will consider how the virtual environment influences attention, interaction, and participation, and why effective online learning requires deliberate planning.

Adapting delivery and facilitation skills

Discover how to transfer established training and facilitation techniques into a virtual environment while maintaining a positive learning experience.

Topics include:

- Applying TAP® delivery principles to virtual environments
- Creating a positive virtual learning climate
- Encouraging interaction and participation online
- Managing learner engagement throughout a session
- Recognising and avoiding virtual fatigue
- Supporting collaboration and discussion

You will explore practical ways to encourage participation, maintain attention, and create opportunities for learners to contribute in an online setting.

Designing effective virtual learning experiences

Learn how to structure virtual learning activities around clear learning needs and outcomes. Consider how the right combination of delivery techniques, resources, and technology can support participation and understanding.

Topics include:

- Applying the TAP® Virtual Delivery Structure
- Adapting classroom learning activities for virtual delivery
- Selecting technology to support learning outcomes
- Considering accessibility and inclusion
- Managing cognitive load in virtual environments
- Preparing resources and learner activities

You will examine how design decisions influence the learner experience and how to use technology purposefully rather than relying on features alone. The focus is on creating accessible, well-structured learning activities that support engagement and learning.

Virtual learning showcase

Apply the principles covered during the programme by creating and presenting a portion of virtual learning on a subject of your choice.

Topics include:

- Designing a practical virtual learning activity
- Showcasing your activity to the group
- Applying the TAP® Virtual Delivery Criteria

The showcase gives you an opportunity to demonstrate your approach to virtual delivery and receive feedback against the programme's criteria. You will use this feedback to identify what works well and where further development may be beneficial.

Course close and next steps

Topics include:

- Creating a personal action plan
- Applying virtual delivery skills in the workplace
- Identifying continuing professional development opportunities
- Reviewing TAP® accreditation and digital badge requirements

You will leave with identified development actions to help you continue improving your virtual training and facilitation practice.

### Exams and assessments

Assessment is based on practical application rather than a specified formal examination.

Throughout the programme, you will participate in virtual learning activities, design an activity on a topic of your choice, and showcase it to the group. You will receive structured feedback from peers and the facilitator and demonstrate how your activity applies the TAP® Virtual Delivery Criteria.

Reflection and action planning will help you identify strengths, areas for improvement, and opportunities to apply your skills in the workplace.

Successful learners will be eligible to achieve the TAP® Accelerated Delivering Virtual Learning Accreditation and progress within the wider TAP® Delivery Excellence Pathway.

The source material does not specify separate examination arrangements or the detailed requirements for issuing the digital badge. These should be confirmed before publication if further detail is required.

### Hands-on learning

Practical application is central to this one-day virtual training course.

You will design and showcase a virtual learning activity, apply TAP® Virtual Delivery principles, and receive structured peer and facilitator feedback. Activities will help you explore learner engagement, adapt delivery techniques, and consider how technology, accessibility, and cognitive load influence online learning.

The programme connects learning to your own delivery practice, helping you identify practical improvements you can take back into the workplace.

## Learning outcomes

By the end of the course, you will be able to:

- Explain the factors that influence engagement and participation in virtual learning
- Apply the TAP® Virtual Delivery Structure to online learning activities
- Adapt classroom training and facilitated activities for virtual environments
- Create a positive and inclusive virtual learning experience
- Select technology based on learning needs and intended outcomes
- Apply accessibility and cognitive load principles when designing virtual learning
- Prepare the technical and practical elements required for successful virtual delivery
- Design and showcase a virtual learning activity using the TAP® Virtual Delivery Criteria

Your practical outcome will be a showcased portion of virtual learning on a subject of your choice, developed in line with the TAP® Virtual Delivery Criteria.

title: Arden Cares | Arden University
text:
Arden Cares is a dedicated support service for students in the UK who have experience of being in care, including those who have spent time in foster care or residential care, those who identify as care leavers, and students who are estranged from their families.

We're here to help you feel supported, build on your strengths, and make the most of your time at Arden, whether you're starting your journey with us or already studying.

We recognise that every student comes to university with different experiences, responsibilities, and challenges. We also understand that some students may not have access to family support and may face additional challenges during their studies.

Arden Cares is here to make sure you always have somewhere to turn for guidance, encouragement and personalised support throughout your time with us.

Whether you're care-experienced, a care leaver or estranged from your family, we're here to support you throughout your Arden journey.

### Who Arden Cares supports

#### Arden Cares is here for:

- Care-experienced students.
- Care leaver students.
- Estranged students.

#### You may be considered care-experienced if you have:

- Spent any time in care or been supported by children’s services at any point in your life.
- Experienced foster care, residential care, or kinship care (living with relatives or family friends)
- Been adopted after time in care.

#### You may be considered a care leaver if:

- You were in care on or after your 14th birthday, and
- You are currently aged 16–25.

If you’re unsure whether you have care leaver status, you can check with your leaving care team or personal adviser, or visit the Am I a care leaver? - Coram Voice website for further guidance.

#### Who is an estranged student?

#### Estranged Students

- You may be considered an estranged student if you are studying without the support and approval of your parents due to an irreconcilable breakdown in your relationship. This means you are no longer in contact with or supported by either of your parents, including biological, adoptive or step-parents, and you may also be estranged from wider family members who have previously been involved in your care.
- Estrangement may have occurred before you started university or during your studies.

#### Not sure if Arden Cares is for you?

That is completely okay. Many students are not certain whether they are considered care-experienced, a care leaver or estranged from their family.

If you think this might apply to you, we encourage you to get in touch. We will talk things through confidentially and without judgement and help you understand what support is available. You're very welcome to get in touch at ardencares@arden.ac.uk.

### What support does Arden Cares offer?

Access to the Care-Experienced and Estranged Student Bursary, subject to eligibility criteria, to help with the costs associated with studying.

Students registered with Arden Cares can access a range of tailored support, which may include:

- A named point of contact for advice, guidance, or simply someone to listen.
- Support with accessing wellbeing, disability, or mental health services.
- One-to-one support with settling into university, study skills, wellbeing, or financial guidance.
- Exclusive events and peer networks to connect with other care-experienced and care leaver students.
- Mentoring, careers support, and internship opportunities to help you prepare for your future.

Support is flexible and can change over time — we will work with you to make sure it continues to meet your needs.

### Financial support

Students registered with Arden Cares may also be eligible for additional financial support, including the Care-Experienced and Estranged Student Bursary for eligible UK undergraduate students.

Eligible full-time students can receive £1,200 per academic year, paid in two instalments of £600. Part-time students may also be eligible for a pro-rata amount. The bursary is subject to eligibility criteria, continued study and regular attendance.

For more information about the Care-Experienced and Estranged Student Bursary and other financial support available, please visit our Cost of Living portal.

### Get in touch with Arden Cares

To find out more about Arden Cares or to register for support, please contact our Care-Experienced, Care Leaver and Estranged Student Support Team:

ardencares@arden.ac.uk

You belong at Arden, and we are here to make sure you feel supported, connected, and ready to thrive.

### Meet your named contact.

Emma Vance – Wellbeing Advisor

Emma is the named contact for Arden Cares and is passionate about ensuring that care-experienced and care leaver students feel supported throughout their journey at Arden University.

She works closely with students to make sure the right support is in place at the right time, offering guidance, a listening ear, and advocacy where needed. Emma believes that care-experienced students should be supported to thrive, not just survive and is committed to walking alongside you throughout your time at Arden.

Sarah-Jayne - Wellbeing Advisor

Sarah-Jayne is the named contact for estranged students at Arden University and is passionate about ensuring that students who are studying independently from their family or support networks feel understood, supported and able to thrive throughout their university journey.

She works closely with students to understand their individual circumstances and help make sure the right support is in place at the right time. This may include guidance around university processes, wellbeing, practical support, reasonable adjustments, and connecting students with other services where needed.

Sarah-Jayne believes that being estranged should never mean having to navigate university alone. She is committed to providing a safe, approachable space where students can talk openly, access the support they need and feel confident throughout their time at Arden.

# Going global: getting career-ready through travel and networking

27 November 2026

Gemma is a true example of grabbing all the opportunities presented to her and a strong representation of what the career-ready revolution stands for.

During her time at Solent, BA (Hons) Business Management and Marketing graduate gained a large range of work experience and grew her industry connections. From working alongside her studies as a student ambassador, through live briefs with real industry clients and even international travel opportunities Gemma got a well-rounded Solent experience to set her up for a successful career.

“On my course one thing that is really good is they are based with real world clients. So last year we did one with Heathrow, this year we actually did one with Think Engine as well.”

Following on from the guest lecture from Solent alumni Ben Michaelis from Think Engine a local Southampton business, Gemma took it a step further by reaching leading to weekly one-to-one mentoring and invitation to networking events.

You don’t often think you can travel the world and build your CV at the same time, however Gemma is a great example as someone who has done exactly that. Gemma utilised Solent’s Turing finding to make the most of the international opportunities which included volunteering in Fiji as part of the sport development project with Think Pacific.

“It was an experience which I developed so many transferable skills from and improved my communication, teamwork and problem-solving skills. I learned how to adapt to a completely new environment and gain confidence working with people from different cultures and backgrounds.”

Not stopping there, she went on to spend two summers as a female sport specialists in America, through Skilled Summers.

“This role taught me how to lead activities, manage groups, think on my feet and take responsibility in a fast-paced environment, whilst also being involved in many random side quests. Following this, I became a Campus Manager with Skilled Summers attending events across the South Coast, delivering presentations and promoting opportunities to students.

What's even better is that I've been able to do all this while studying for my degree, making the most of the funding and opportunities available to me.”

After graduating with a first-class degree, Gemma feels prepared and excited for the next chapter of her journey.

“I've been able to travel whilst also building up my CV likewise have made amazing memories, alongside gaining the skills and confidence to be career ready for whatever comes next.”

# Solent Dean to help shape future academic leaders across UK business schools

27 November 2026

A senior leader at Southampton Solent University has been appointed to co-design and deliver a new national programme supporting the next generation of academic leaders in business education.

Professor Lois Farquharson, Dean of the School of Business, Law and Society, has been invited by the Chartered Association of Business Schools (CABS) to co-lead its new Academic Leadership and Management Programme (ALMP), alongside Professor Stuart Hyde from Alliance Manchester Business School at the University of Manchester.

As the representative body for UK business schools, CABS works to champion excellence in business and management education and develop leadership capability across the higher education sector.

The residential programme will bring together current and aspiring academic leaders from business schools across the UK. Through practical workshops, strategic simulations and collaborative learning, participants will develop the skills and confidence needed to lead teams, make strategic decisions and navigate the challenges facing higher education.

Professor Farquharson said:

“I am delighted to be working with Stuart and the Chartered Association of Business Schools to develop and deliver this national programme. Effective academic leadership has never been more important. This programme provides an opportunity to share experience, challenge thinking and equip current and future academic leaders with the confidence and capabilities to make a positive difference within their institutions and across the wider sector.”

Professor Farquharson’s appointment reflects her extensive experience in business school leadership, academic strategy, organisational transformation and leadership development. A CMI Chartered Companion, she brings significant expertise to a programme designed to strengthen leadership across one of the UK’s most important sectors.

The appointment also highlights Southampton Solent University’s growing influence within the higher education sector and its commitment to developing leaders who can drive positive change.

As a university renowned for its career-ready, practice-led approach to education, Solent works closely with industry and professional bodies to ensure its students and staff develop the skills, knowledge and leadership capabilities needed to succeed. Professor Farquharson’s role in shaping a national leadership programme reinforces the University’s reputation for combining academic excellence with real-world impact and professional practice.

By helping to develop future leaders across UK business schools, Solent is contributing to the strength of higher education nationally while further enhancing its profile as a university that prepares people to make a meaningful difference in their professions and communities.
